title: Public vs Private Companies: Key Differences
excerpt: Public companies sell shares to anyone through a stock exchange and must disclose detailed financials; private companies keep ownership closely held and their books largely confidential.

content.html: Every company starts private. Founders, early employees, and sometimes venture investors hold all the shares, and there's no public market to trade them on. Some companies stay that way forever; others eventually go public, listing shares on an exchange where anyone can buy in.

content.text: What Makes a Company Public

content.html: A public company has sold shares to the general public, usually through an initial public offering, and those shares now trade on an exchange like the NYSE or Nasdaq. Going public gives a company access to a much larger pool of capital and liquidity for its early investors, but it comes with an entirely new set of legal obligations.
Public companies must file detailed, regular financial reports with the SEC, hold shareholder meetings, and generally operate under far more scrutiny than a private business ever would.

content.text: What Makes a Company Private

content.html: A private company's shares are held by a limited group — founders, employees, private equity or venture capital firms, and sometimes family members — and are not available for the general public to buy on an open market. Private companies still have shareholders and can still issue stock, but transferring those shares typically requires the company's approval and isn't nearly as liquid as trading on an exchange.

content.text: Private doesn't mean small: Some of the largest, most valuable companies in the world remain privately held for years, often specifically to avoid the disclosure and short-term pressure that comes with public markets.
Disclosure and Transparency Differences

content.html: This is the sharpest practical difference. A public company's revenue, profit, debt levels, and executive pay are all a matter of public record, updated quarterly. A private company can keep nearly all of that confidential, sharing detailed financials only with its actual investors and lenders, not the general public.
Core differences at a glance

content.text: How a Private Company Goes Public

content.html: The most common route is an IPO, where the company works with investment banks to price and sell an initial batch of shares to institutional and retail investors. Some companies instead use a direct listing, skipping the traditional underwriting process, or merge with a special purpose acquisition company. Whatever the route, going public means accepting far greater ongoing transparency in exchange for access to public capital.

content.text: Can Regular Investors Buy Private Company Stock?

content.html: Generally, no — not easily. Private company shares are typically restricted to accredited investors, employees, or institutional funds, though some newer platforms have opened limited access to private equity for retail investors under specific SEC exemptions. For most people, exposure to a private company only becomes possible once it goes public.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Public companies sell shares on an open exchange; private companies restrict ownership to a limited group.
  • Public companies face extensive SEC disclosure requirements; private companies keep financials largely confidential.
  • Public shares are far more liquid, trading daily, while private shares are hard to buy or sell quickly.
  • Going public, usually through an IPO, trades increased transparency for access to broader capital markets.
  • Regular retail investors generally can't buy private company shares until that company goes public.
  • Some very large, well-known companies choose to stay private for years to avoid public market pressure.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What is the main difference between a public and private company?

content.html: The core difference is whether shares are available for the general public to buy on a stock exchange. Public companies are, and face heavy financial disclosure requirements as a result; private companies restrict ownership and keep most financials confidential.

content.text: Why would a company choose to stay private?

content.html: Staying private avoids the cost and scrutiny of SEC reporting, lets management focus on long-term decisions without quarterly earnings pressure, and keeps competitors from seeing detailed financial data.

content.text: How do employees at private companies get paid in equity?

content.html: Private companies commonly issue stock options or restricted stock units that vest over time. These shares are illiquid until the company goes public or is acquired, at which point employees can typically sell them.

content.text: What happens to outstanding shares when a company goes public?

content.html: Existing private shares typically convert into public shares of the same or a related class, and new shares are issued and sold in the offering. See our guide on outstanding shares for how total share counts are tracked and reported.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: The public-private divide comes down to a trade: public companies gain access to enormous pools of capital and liquidity in exchange for detailed, ongoing disclosure; private companies keep control and confidentiality but accept a smaller, less liquid pool of potential investors. Neither structure is inherently better — it depends entirely on what a company, and its owners, actually need.

title: Revenue: What It Means for a Public Company
excerpt: Revenue is the total amount of money a company brings in from selling its products or services, before any expenses are subtracted — the starting line of the income statement.

content.html: Every income statement, no matter the industry, starts in the same place: revenue. It's the total amount of money a company generated from its core business activity during a given period, before rent, salaries, taxes, or anything else gets subtracted. Investors often call it the 'top line' precisely because of where it sits on the page.
Revenue gets treated as a simple number, but reading it well means understanding what counts, what doesn't, and why a growing top line doesn't automatically mean a healthier company underneath it.

content.text: What Actually Counts as Revenue

content.html: Revenue includes money earned from a company's primary business operations — selling products, providing services, or licensing something the company owns. It's recognized under accounting rules when a good or service has actually been delivered, not necessarily when cash changes hands, which is why revenue and cash received in a given period can differ. Money from one-time events like selling off a building or a legal settlement typically isn't counted as revenue at all; it shows up elsewhere on the financial statements as a separate gain or loss.

content.text: A Worked Example

content.html: Here's a simplified illustration of how revenue sits at the top of an income statement, before anything else is subtracted.
Illustrative example — not real company data

content.text: Revenue is only the starting point: In this example, only 12% of every revenue dollar ultimately became profit. A company can post huge revenue and still be unprofitable if its costs run higher than what it brings in.
What Healthy Revenue Growth Looks Like

content.html: There's no universal growth rate that defines 'good' revenue performance, since it depends heavily on company size, industry, and stage of maturity. Directionally, consistent revenue growth over multiple years — rather than one standout quarter followed by stagnation — tends to reflect a more durable business. Larger, established companies typically grow revenue more slowly in percentage terms than smaller or newer companies, simply because it takes a much bigger dollar amount to move the needle at scale.

content.text: Where to Find It

content.html: Revenue sits at the very top of the income statement in every 10-Q and 10-K filed with the SEC, sometimes labeled 'net sales' or 'total revenue' depending on the industry. Companies with multiple business segments often break revenue down by segment or geography elsewhere in the filing, which can reveal whether growth is broad-based or concentrated in just one part of the business.

content.text: Limitations of Looking at Revenue Alone

content.html: Revenue says nothing about profitability — a company can grow sales aggressively while losing money on every transaction, particularly common among young, growth-focused companies prioritizing market share. It also doesn't account for how that revenue was generated; heavy discounting or one-time bulk deals can inflate a single quarter's revenue without reflecting the sustainable demand for the underlying product. That's why revenue is almost always read alongside profitability metrics like net income and free cash flow rather than treated as a standalone signal of company health.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Revenue is the total money earned from a company's core business, recognized before expenses and before cash necessarily changes hands.
  • It excludes one-time gains like asset sales, which are recorded separately from operating revenue.
  • Consistent multi-year revenue growth generally signals a more durable business than a single strong quarter.
  • Revenue is disclosed at the top of the income statement in every 10-Q and 10-K SEC filing.
  • High revenue doesn't guarantee profitability — costs can exceed revenue even at large sales volumes.
  • Revenue is most useful when read alongside profitability and cash flow metrics, not in isolation.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Is revenue the same as profit?

content.html: No. Revenue is the total money brought in from sales before any costs are subtracted. Profit (net income) is what remains after subtracting all expenses, taxes, and other costs from revenue. A company can have high revenue and still report a net loss.

content.text: Why do investors care about revenue growth specifically?

content.html: Sustained revenue growth is often an early sign of increasing demand for a company's products or services, which can eventually translate into higher profits if the business manages its costs effectively as it scales.

content.text: What's the difference between revenue and cash flow?

content.html: Revenue is recognized when a sale happens, which can occur before cash is actually received (for example, on credit terms). Cash flow tracks the actual movement of cash in and out of the business, which is why the two figures can diverge in a given period.

content.text: Can a company have revenue but no profit?

content.html: Yes, and it's common among younger, fast-growing companies. If operating costs, marketing spend, or interest expenses exceed revenue, the company posts a net loss despite having substantial top-line sales.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Revenue is where every company's financial story begins, but it's only the opening chapter. A rising top line is encouraging, but it only becomes meaningful once you check what happened to that money as it flowed down through costs, taxes, and other expenses toward the bottom line.

title: Risk Management for Stock Investors
excerpt: Risk management in stock investing isn't about eliminating losses — it's a set of practical habits that keep any single mistake from derailing your overall plan.

content.html: Every stock investment carries risk, and no amount of research eliminates that fact. Risk management isn't about finding some trick that removes risk from the equation — it's a set of practical habits that keep any single bad outcome from being the one that actually hurts you.
The investors who last decades in the market usually aren't the ones who avoided every loss. They're the ones who structured their portfolios so no individual loss could do lasting damage.

content.text: Risk Isn't the Same as Volatility

content.html: Volatility is how much a stock's price moves around; risk is the chance of a permanent, meaningful loss of capital. A stock can be volatile day to day and still be a perfectly reasonable long-term holding, while a stable-looking stock in a declining business can carry more real risk than its calm price chart suggests.
Conflating the two leads to bad decisions — selling a volatile but fundamentally sound stock out of discomfort, or holding a quietly deteriorating one because it hasn't moved much yet.

content.text: Position Sizing: Your First Line of Defense

content.html: Position sizing means deciding, in advance, how much of your portfolio any single stock is allowed to represent. Even a stock you're highly confident in shouldn't dominate your holdings, because confidence isn't a guarantee, and companies that looked unshakeable have failed before.

A common guideline caps any single stock at somewhere around 5-10% of a portfolio for individual investors, though this varies by risk tolerance and how much of the portfolio is otherwise diversified through funds.

content.text: Concentration cuts both ways: A concentrated bet can produce outsized gains, but it produces outsized losses with equal ease. Position sizing is how you decide how much of that swing you can actually afford.
Diversification as Structural Risk Management

content.html: Spreading money across companies, sectors, and asset classes remains one of the most reliable risk management tools available to ordinary investors, since it directly limits the damage any single bad outcome can do. Our full guide on diversification covers how to think about spreading risk across your holdings.

Your broader mix between stocks, bonds, and cash — covered in our guide on portfolio allocation basics — is another layer of the same idea, applied at the asset-class level rather than the individual-stock level.

content.text: Setting Rules Before You Need Them

content.html: The best risk management decisions happen before you're emotionally invested in the outcome. Deciding in advance how much you're willing to lose on a position, under what conditions you'd sell, and how large any one holding is allowed to grow all remove pressure from moments when your judgment is least reliable.
Some investors use a mental or literal stop-loss threshold; others rely more on periodic portfolio reviews. Either approach beats deciding in the moment, with a red number flashing on the screen.
Risk Management Tools at a Glance

content.text: Risk Management Doesn't Mean Playing It Too Safe

content.html: Being overly conservative carries its own risk — inflation erodes cash sitting on the sidelines, and an overly cautious portfolio may not grow enough to meet long-term goals like retirement. Good risk management balances protecting against loss with taking on enough risk to actually make progress, rather than avoiding stocks altogether.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Volatility and risk are related but different — a price that moves a lot isn't automatically a bad investment.
  • Position sizing limits how much damage any single stock can do to your overall portfolio.
  • Diversification across companies and sectors is one of the most reliable risk management tools available.
  • Your stock, bond, and cash allocation manages risk at the broader asset-class level.
  • Deciding your rules before a downturn hits removes pressure from your least reliable moments.
  • Being too conservative carries its own risk, including inflation eroding returns over time.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What is the biggest risk management mistake new investors make?

content.html: Concentrating too much money in a single stock, often one they feel strongly about, without limiting position size. Even good companies occasionally fail or underperform for reasons no one predicted in advance.

content.text: Should I use stop-loss orders to manage risk?

content.html: Stop-loss orders can limit downside on individual positions, but they can also trigger sales during short-term volatility in a fundamentally sound stock. Many long-term investors prefer position sizing and diversification over relying on automatic stop-losses.

content.text: How much of my portfolio should be in one stock?

content.html: A commonly cited guideline caps individual stock positions around 5-10% of a portfolio, though the right number depends on your overall diversification, risk tolerance, and how much of your portfolio sits in broader index funds.

content.text: Is it possible to eliminate investment risk entirely?

content.html: No. Even cash carries the risk of losing purchasing power to inflation over time. Risk management aims to size and diversify risk sensibly, not eliminate it, since some risk is necessary to generate meaningful long-term returns.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Managing risk as a stock investor isn't about finding a formula that guarantees you'll never lose money — that formula doesn't exist. It's about sizing positions sensibly, diversifying across companies and asset classes, and deciding your rules before a downturn tests your resolve. Investors who last aren't the ones who avoided every loss; they're the ones who made sure no single loss could take them out of the game.

title: Return on Assets (ROA) Explained
excerpt: Return on assets measures how efficiently a company generates profit from everything it owns, calculated by dividing net income by total assets — debt-funded or not.

content.html: Return on equity tells you how efficiently a company uses shareholder money, but it has a well-known blind spot: it ignores debt entirely, which means a heavily leveraged company can post an impressive ROE without actually running a more efficient operation. Return on assets, or ROA, closes that gap by measuring profit against everything a company owns, regardless of whether it was funded by shareholders or by borrowed money.

Because it accounts for the full asset base, ROA is especially useful for comparing companies with different debt levels, or for judging a single company's efficiency trend without the distortion leverage can introduce.

content.text: The Formula, Explained

content.html: Return on assets equals net income divided by average total assets, typically expressed as a percentage. Average total assets is calculated by averaging the beginning and ending total asset figures from the balance sheet for the period being measured. A 6% ROA means the company generated 6 cents of profit for every dollar of assets it controls, whether those assets were purchased with cash, debt, or reinvested profit.

content.text: A Worked Example

content.html: Here's how the calculation plays out, and how it can tell a different story than ROE for the same company.
Illustrative example — not real company data

content.text: A wider asset base isn't automatically an advantage: Company X needed two and a half times more total assets than Company Y to produce the same profit — a clear sign of lower asset efficiency, even if both companies reported similar ROE figures.
What a Reasonable ROA Range Looks Like

content.html: ROA tends to run structurally lower for asset-heavy industries — banks, utilities, manufacturers — since they need large asset bases just to operate, while asset-light businesses like software or consulting firms often post much higher ROA because they require relatively few assets to generate revenue. This makes cross-industry ROA comparisons close to meaningless; the more useful comparison is a company against direct competitors in its own industry, or against its own historical trend.

content.text: Where to Find and Calculate It

content.html: Net income comes from the income statement, and total assets come from the balance sheet, both available in a company's 10-Q or 10-K filing with the SEC. Average the beginning and ending total assets for the period, divide net income by that figure, and you have ROA. As with ROE, most finance platforms calculate this for you automatically, though understanding the inputs helps you spot when a change in ROA is driven by a shift in profit versus a shift in the asset base.

content.text: Limitations Worth Remembering

content.html: ROA doesn't account for how effectively a company is using leverage to boost shareholder returns — a company using debt intelligently might show a modest ROA while still delivering strong returns to equity holders through ROE. It's also, like other ratios built on net income, sensitive to accounting choices around depreciation and one-time items that can temporarily inflate or depress the numerator without reflecting a real change in how efficiently assets are being used. And because ROA varies so much by industry, using it to compare a bank against a software company tells you almost nothing useful.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• ROA = net income ÷ average total assets, expressed as a percentage.
  • Unlike ROE, it isn't distorted by how much debt a company carries, since it measures against all assets.
  • Asset-heavy industries structurally post lower ROA than asset-light ones, so cross-industry comparisons are unreliable.
  • Net income and total assets both come from a company's 10-Q or 10-K SEC filing.
  • ROA is best compared against direct industry peers or a company's own historical trend.
  • Pairing ROA with ROE reveals how much of a company's shareholder return comes from leverage versus genuine efficiency.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What is considered a good ROA?

content.html: It depends heavily on the industry — asset-light businesses naturally post higher ROA than asset-heavy ones like banks or manufacturers. Compare a company's ROA against direct competitors and its own historical range rather than against a universal number.

content.text: Why is ROA usually lower than ROE for the same company?

content.html: Total assets typically exceed shareholders' equity because assets are funded partly by debt in addition to equity. Since ROA divides by the larger figure, it's mathematically almost always lower than ROE for any company carrying debt.

content.text: Is ROA better than ROE?

content.html: Neither is universally better — they measure different things. ROA isolates operating efficiency from financing decisions, while ROE reflects the return actually delivered to shareholders, including the effects of leverage. Using both together gives a more complete picture.

content.text: Can ROA be used to compare companies in different industries?

content.html: Not reliably. Asset-heavy and asset-light industries have structurally different ROA ranges, so comparing a utility company's ROA to a software company's ROA says more about industry structure than about which is better managed.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Return on assets strips out the effect of financing decisions and asks a more basic question: how much profit is a company generating from everything it actually owns? That makes it a valuable cross-check against ROE, especially for spotting whether a company's returns are driven by genuine operating efficiency or by leaning on debt.

title: Return on Equity (ROE) Explained
excerpt: Return on equity measures how efficiently a company turns shareholders' invested capital into profit, calculated by dividing net income by shareholders' equity.

content.html: Two companies can post identical net income figures and still be run very differently under the hood — one might be generating that profit from a lean base of shareholder capital, while the other needed far more invested equity to get there. Return on equity, or ROE, is the metric built specifically to surface that difference.

It's a favorite of value investors and famously one of Warren Buffett's preferred screening tools, because it gets at something P/E and revenue growth alone can't show: how efficiently management is putting shareholders' money to work.

content.text: The Formula, Explained

content.html: Return on equity equals net income divided by average shareholders' equity, typically expressed as a percentage. In plain terms: for every dollar shareholders have invested in the company (as reflected on the balance sheet), how many cents of profit did the business generate over the period? A 15% ROE means the company generated 15 cents of profit for every dollar of shareholder equity.

Using average shareholders' equity — the beginning and ending balance for the period, averaged together — rather than just the ending figure gives a slightly more accurate picture, since equity can change meaningfully over the course of a year through profits retained, dividends paid, or share buybacks.

content.text: A Worked Example

content.html: Here's how two hypothetical companies with the same profit can post very different ROE figures.
Illustrative example — not real company data

content.text: Same profit, very different efficiency: Company X generated the same total profit as Company Y using less than half the shareholder capital — a meaningfully more efficient use of invested equity, at least on this measure alone.
What a Reasonable ROE Range Looks Like

content.html: There's no universal target ROE, since it varies by industry and by how much debt a company carries — more on that limitation shortly. Directionally, a consistently higher ROE relative to industry peers, sustained over several years rather than a single standout period, is generally viewed as a sign of efficient management and a durable competitive position. Very low or negative ROE across multiple years is worth investigating, though it can sometimes reflect a temporary rough patch rather than a permanent problem.

content.text: Where to Find and Calculate It

content.html: Net income comes from the income statement; shareholders' equity comes from the balance sheet — both found in a company's 10-Q or 10-K SEC filing. Average the beginning and ending shareholders' equity figures for the period, divide net income by that average, and you have ROE. Most financial data platforms calculate this automatically, but confirming it yourself is useful when a company's equity has shifted significantly due to a large buyback or capital raise.

content.text: Limitations to Keep in Mind

content.html: The biggest catch with ROE is that it can be inflated simply by taking on more debt: borrowing money doesn't add to shareholders' equity, but if that borrowed capital generates additional profit, ROE rises without the company necessarily becoming more efficient — it's become more leveraged instead. This is why ROE is best evaluated alongside a company's debt levels, and often compared against return on assets (ROA), which isn't affected by leverage in the same way and can reveal whether a high ROE reflects genuine efficiency or simply higher risk-taking.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• ROE = net income ÷ average shareholders' equity, expressed as a percentage.
  • It measures how efficiently a company converts shareholder capital into profit.
  • A consistently higher ROE than industry peers, sustained over years, often signals efficient management.
  • Net income and shareholders' equity both come from a company's 10-Q or 10-K SEC filing.
  • Taking on more debt can artificially inflate ROE without making the business genuinely more efficient.
  • Pairing ROE with return on assets helps reveal whether high ROE reflects efficiency or leverage.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What is considered a good ROE?

content.html: There's no fixed universal benchmark since it varies by industry and capital structure. A useful approach is comparing a company's ROE to its direct competitors and to its own multi-year trend, rather than to one number across the whole market.

content.text: Why can ROE be misleading for heavily indebted companies?

content.html: Debt isn't part of shareholders' equity, so a company can boost ROE by borrowing money and using it to generate additional profit, without any real gain in operating efficiency. Checking debt levels alongside ROE helps you tell the two apart.

content.text: What's the difference between ROE and ROA?

content.html: ROE measures return relative to shareholders' equity alone, while ROA measures return relative to total assets, including those funded by debt. ROA isn't distorted by leverage the way ROE can be, making the two metrics useful complements.

content.text: Can ROE be negative?

content.html: Yes, if a company reports a net loss for the period, ROE turns negative. A single negative period isn't necessarily alarming, but a sustained negative or declining ROE trend across multiple years is worth investigating further.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Return on equity is a genuinely useful shorthand for management efficiency, but its one major blind spot — sensitivity to debt — means it should never be read entirely on its own. Check it against a company's debt levels and its return on assets, and you'll get a far more reliable read on whether a high ROE reflects real operating skill or simply financial leverage.

title: Relative Strength Index (RSI) Explained
excerpt: The Relative Strength Index gauges how fast and how far a stock has moved recently, flagging conditions traders commonly call overbought or oversold.

content.html: The Relative Strength Index, universally shortened to RSI, is a momentum indicator that measures the speed and size of recent price changes to judge whether a stock has moved unusually far, unusually fast. Developed by J. Welles Wilder in the late 1970s, it's become one of the most widely referenced indicators in technical analysis, largely because it's plotted on a simple 0-to-100 scale that's easy to read at a glance.

content.text: How RSI Is Actually Calculated

content.html: RSI compares the average size of a stock's up days to the average size of its down days over a set lookback period, most commonly 14 periods. That ratio gets converted into a 0-to-100 scale: readings closer to 100 mean recent gains have dominated recent losses by a wide margin, while readings closer to 0 mean the opposite. You don't need to run the formula by hand — every charting platform plots it automatically — but understanding that it's a ratio of gains to losses, not a price level itself, makes the number far less mysterious.

content.text: Overbought and Oversold Thresholds

content.html: The conventional reading treats RSI above 70 as overbought — suggesting a stock may have risen too far, too fast, and could be due for a pause or pullback — and RSI below 30 as oversold, suggesting the opposite. These are conventions, not hard rules; some traders use 80/20 for a stricter read, and a genuinely strong trending stock can sit above 70 for weeks without ever pulling back.
Commonly cited RSI thresholds (conventions, not fixed rules)

rows: Often treated as a rough midpoint, sometimes used as a trend filter
Stricter thresholds some traders prefer for fewer, higher-conviction signals

content.text: Overbought doesn't mean sell: A stock in a strong uptrend can stay 'overbought' by RSI's definition for a long stretch. Treat the 70/30 thresholds as a prompt to look closer, not an automatic trading signal.
RSI Divergence: The More Nuanced Signal

content.html: Divergence happens when price and RSI move in opposite directions — for example, a stock makes a new high while RSI makes a lower high than its previous peak, suggesting the upward momentum behind the move is weakening even though price is still climbing. Bearish divergence like this, and its mirror-image bullish version at market lows, is considered by many technical traders to be a more meaningful signal than the raw overbought/oversold reading alone, though it's also harder to spot consistently and prone to being seen in hindsight where it wasn't clearly there in real time.

content.text: Where RSI Gets Traders Into Trouble

content.html: The most common mistake is treating an overbought reading as an automatic sell signal in a strong trend, which routinely leads to exiting or shorting a stock that keeps climbing for weeks afterward. RSI also produces noisier, less useful signals in choppy, low-volatility markets, and like most tools built from recent price history, it says more about what's already happened than what happens next. Pairing RSI with moving averages for trend context, or MACD for a second momentum read, is standard practice for reducing false signals rather than relying on RSI in isolation.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• RSI measures the ratio of recent gains to recent losses on a 0-to-100 scale, most commonly over a 14-period lookback.
  • Readings above 70 are conventionally called overbought and below 30 oversold — these are conventions, not fixed rules.
  • A stock can stay 'overbought' for a long stretch during a genuinely strong trend without reversing.
  • Divergence between price and RSI direction is considered a more nuanced, sometimes more meaningful signal than the raw threshold.
  • RSI performs worse in choppy, low-volatility markets and works best combined with trend or other momentum tools.
  • Like all technical indicators built from past prices, RSI describes recent behavior more confidently than it predicts future moves.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What does RSI above 70 mean?

content.html: It's conventionally read as an overbought condition, suggesting a stock has risen quickly relative to its recent history. It's not an automatic sell signal — strong trending stocks can remain above 70 for extended stretches.

content.text: What is RSI divergence?

content.html: Divergence occurs when price and RSI move in opposite directions, such as price making a new high while RSI makes a lower high. It's considered a possible sign that momentum behind a price move is weakening, though it's harder to spot reliably in real time than in hindsight.

content.text: What's the best RSI period to use?

content.html: 14 periods is the original and most widely used setting. Shorter periods make RSI more sensitive and noisier; longer periods smooth it out but react more slowly to new price action.

content.text: Can RSI be used alone to trade stocks?

content.html: It's generally not recommended as a standalone tool. Most traders combine RSI with trend indicators like moving averages, or confirm signals with volume, since RSI alone produces frequent false signals, especially in trending or choppy markets.

content.text: Is RSI the same as MACD?

content.html: No. Both are momentum indicators, but they're built differently and often used together rather than as substitutes — see our separate guide to MACD for how it differs from RSI.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: RSI gives traders a simple, standardized way to gauge whether a stock's recent move has been unusually fast or far relative to its own history, which is genuinely useful context. The failure mode is treating the 70/30 thresholds as automatic trading triggers rather than conventions worth checking against the broader trend — a stock can stay overbought through weeks of a strong rally, and oversold through weeks of a genuine decline.

faq.question: What does RSI above 70 mean?
faq.answer: It's conventionally read as an overbought condition, suggesting a stock has risen quickly relative to its recent history. It's not an automatic sell signal — strong trending stocks can remain above 70 for extended stretches.

faq.question: What is RSI divergence?
faq.answer: Divergence occurs when price and RSI move in opposite directions, such as price making a new high while RSI makes a lower high. It's considered a possible sign that momentum behind a price move is weakening, though it's harder to spot reliably in real time than in hindsight.

faq.question: What's the best RSI period to use?
faq.answer: 14 periods is the original and most widely used setting. Shorter periods make RSI more sensitive and noisier; longer periods smooth it out but react more slowly to new price action.

faq.question: Can RSI be used alone to trade stocks?
faq.answer: It's generally not recommended as a standalone tool. Most traders combine RSI with trend indicators like moving averages, or confirm signals with volume, since RSI alone produces frequent false signals, especially in trending or choppy markets.

faq.question: Is RSI the same as MACD?
faq.answer: No. Both are momentum indicators, but they're built differently and often used together rather than as substitutes — see our separate guide to MACD for how it differs from RSI.

title: Shareholder Voting Rights Explained
excerpt: Owning common stock typically grants voting rights on major corporate decisions, exercised at annual meetings or through mailed and electronic proxy ballots.

content.html: If you own common stock, you've probably received an email or envelope around proxy season asking you to vote on things like board nominees or an executive pay package. Most people click through it quickly, or ignore it entirely — but that ballot represents a real, if usually small, piece of corporate control.

content.text: What Shareholders Actually Vote On

content.html: Common shareholders typically vote on electing directors to the board, approving or rejecting executive compensation packages, ratifying the outside auditor, and weighing in on major structural changes like mergers, stock splits, or amendments to corporate bylaws. Shareholders can also submit their own proposals for a vote, covering everything from environmental policy to governance reforms.

content.text: How Proxy Voting Works in Practice

content.html: Almost nobody attends the actual annual shareholder meeting in person. Instead, companies mail or email a proxy statement, and shareholders vote remotely — by mail, phone, or an online portal — assigning their vote to a proxy who casts it on their behalf according to their instructions. Your brokerage handles the logistics since it's technically the holder of record for shares held in a standard brokerage account.

content.text: Your vote is smaller than you'd think, but real: A retail investor with a few hundred shares won't swing an election alone, but collectively, retail shareholders can and do influence outcomes, especially on close governance votes.
One Share, One Vote — Usually

content.html: The standard rule is one vote per common share, but plenty of companies deviate from it through dual-class share structures, where founders or insiders hold a class of stock with ten or more votes per share, while public investors hold shares with one vote or none. This lets founders retain control even after selling a majority of the company's economic value to the public. Our companion piece on common stock explains how these share classes typically work.

content.text: Do Preferred Shareholders Get to Vote?

content.html: Usually not, or only in limited circumstances — most preferred stock trades voting rights away in exchange for a fixed, prioritized dividend. Some preferred agreements grant voting rights only if the company misses a set number of dividend payments, as a protective mechanism. See our guide on preferred stock for the full mechanics.

content.text: Why Bothering to Vote Still Matters

content.html: Corporate votes on executive pay, board composition, and shareholder proposals have shifted real outcomes at major companies in recent years, particularly on close votes where institutional investors were split. Voting costs nothing and takes a few minutes — skipping it just hands more relative influence to whoever does show up.

content.text: Shareholder Activism and Proposals

content.html: Beyond routine board and pay votes, shareholders — often organized activist investors or advocacy groups — can formally submit proposals asking a company to change a specific practice, from environmental disclosures to compensation structures. These proposals rarely pass outright on the first attempt, but a strong minority vote can pressure a board into voluntarily adopting the change without a formal mandate, since directors generally prefer to avoid a recurring, embarrassing fight at each annual meeting.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Common stock typically grants one vote per share on board elections, mergers, and other major decisions.
  • Most shareholders vote remotely through a proxy ballot rather than attending meetings in person.
  • Dual-class share structures let some companies give insiders outsized voting power relative to ownership.
  • Preferred shareholders usually have limited or no voting rights, unless specific conditions are triggered.
  • Shareholders can submit their own proposals for a vote at the annual meeting.
  • Individual votes are small in isolation but add up meaningfully in aggregate, especially on close votes.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Do I have to vote my shares?

content.html: No, voting is optional. If you don't vote, your shares simply aren't counted, and in some cases your broker may vote them in a default way on routine matters, though not on contested issues.

content.text: How many votes does one share of stock get?

content.html: Typically one vote per common share, but this isn't universal. Some companies use dual-class structures where different share classes carry different voting weights, sometimes ten or more votes per insider-held share.

content.text: Can I vote if I own stock through a mutual fund or ETF?

content.html: Not directly — the fund itself holds the shares and votes on behalf of its investors. Some fund providers now offer pass-through voting programs letting individual investors express preferences, but this remains uncommon.

content.text: What happens if a shareholder vote is close?

content.html: Close votes get resolved by the final tally, same as any election — the outcome that receives the required majority (often a simple majority, sometimes higher for major changes) is adopted, and the result is disclosed publicly.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Shareholder voting is one of the few direct levers ordinary investors have over how a public company is run. It won't feel powerful casting one vote among millions, but the aggregate of engaged shareholders has shaped real corporate decisions — and it costs nothing to participate.

title: Small-Cap Stocks Explained
excerpt: Small-cap stocks are companies with relatively small total market values, offering more room to grow and more risk of failure than their larger counterparts.

content.html: Every large company was small once, and part of the appeal of small-cap stocks is the idea of getting in before the rest of the market notices. Small-cap stocks are shares in companies with a relatively small total market value, or market capitalization, and that smaller size comes with both more room to grow quickly and considerably more risk of the business struggling or failing outright.

The category sits at a genuine inflection point in market-cap investing — smaller than the mid-cap and large-cap companies most index funds are weighted toward, but generally still large enough to trade on a major exchange with real disclosure requirements, unlike the murkier penny stock world.

content.text: What Counts as a Small-Cap Stock

content.html: Market capitalization is calculated by multiplying a company's share price by its total number of outstanding shares, and it's the standard way the market sorts companies by size. While the exact cutoffs shift somewhat by index provider, small-cap generally refers to companies in the lower range of publicly traded market values — smaller than the well-known large-cap names, but still listed on major exchanges.

content.text: Market-Cap Categories at a Glance

content.html: These ranges are commonly used guidelines rather than fixed legal definitions, and different index providers draw the lines slightly differently.
Typical market-cap size categories

content.text: Why Investors Are Drawn to Small-Cap Stocks

content.html: Small companies generally have more room to grow quickly than already-dominant large companies, simply because doubling revenue is a smaller absolute number to achieve from a smaller starting base. Small-cap stocks have historically shown periods of outperforming large-cap stocks over long stretches, particularly coming out of recessions, though that outperformance has come with meaningfully more volatility along the way.

content.text: Small-cap indexes track this category: The Russell 2000 is the most widely cited small-cap benchmark in the U.S. market, tracking roughly the smallest 2,000 companies in the broader Russell 3000 index.
The Risks That Come With Smaller Size

content.html: Small companies typically have less financial cushion to survive a bad year, less access to cheap capital, thinner analyst coverage, and less name recognition to fall back on than large-cap peers. Their stock prices also tend to be more volatile day to day, since smaller trading volumes mean it takes less buying or selling pressure to move the price meaningfully.

content.text: Small-Cap in Context: Related Categories

content.html: Small-cap is one step up from penny stocks in terms of size and disclosure requirements, and one step below mid-cap stocks. Many small-cap companies also carry a growth stock profile, since a smaller company expanding quickly often shows both traits at once.

Because small-cap companies are less thoroughly covered by Wall Street analysts, mispricings can persist longer than they would for a heavily scrutinized large-cap name — which is exactly why some active fund managers specialize in this segment, betting that diligent research can uncover value the broader market hasn't priced in yet. That same lack of coverage cuts both ways, though, since it's also easier for problems at a small company to go unnoticed until they show up directly in the stock price.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Small-cap stocks are companies with a relatively small total market value, roughly $300 million to $2 billion by common convention.
  • Market capitalization is calculated as share price multiplied by total shares outstanding.
  • Small-cap companies generally have more room to grow quickly but considerably more risk than large-cap peers.
  • The Russell 2000 is the most widely followed U.S. small-cap benchmark.
  • Thinner analyst coverage and less financial cushion make small-cap stocks more volatile and harder to research.
  • Small-cap stocks often overlap with the growth stock category, since rapid expansion is common at this size.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What is considered a small-cap stock?

content.html: By common convention, a small-cap stock has a total market capitalization roughly between $300 million and $2 billion, though exact cutoffs vary by index provider and shift over time as markets grow.

content.text: Are small-cap stocks riskier than large-cap stocks?

content.html: Generally yes. Smaller companies have less financial cushion, thinner analyst coverage, and more volatile share prices, though they also carry more potential for rapid growth than already-large companies.

content.text: What index tracks small-cap stocks?

content.html: The Russell 2000 is the most widely cited U.S. small-cap benchmark, tracking roughly the smallest 2,000 companies within the broader Russell 3000 index.

content.text: How is a small-cap stock different from a penny stock?

content.html: Small-cap stocks are typically listed on major exchanges with full disclosure requirements, even though they're smaller companies. Penny stocks trade at very low prices, often over-the-counter with far less reporting oversight.

content.text: Do small-cap stocks pay dividends?

content.html: Less commonly than large-cap or blue-chip stocks, since smaller companies more often reinvest available cash into growing the business rather than distributing it to shareholders.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Small-cap stocks offer a genuine trade — more room to grow in exchange for meaningfully more risk and less predictability than their larger counterparts. They can play a useful role in a diversified portfolio, but position sizing and research matter more here than almost anywhere else in the market-cap spectrum.

title: Stock Certificates: What They Are (And Do You Still Need One)
excerpt: A stock certificate is a paper document proving share ownership. Almost all modern trading skips paper entirely, using electronic book-entry records instead.

content.html: Decades ago, buying stock meant eventually receiving an ornate paper document with your name, the company's, and the number of shares printed across it. That's a stock certificate — and if you've ever inherited one from a relative or seen one framed on an office wall, you've probably wondered whether it's still worth anything or whether you even need one today.

content.text: What a Stock Certificate Actually Is

content.html: A stock certificate is a legal document certifying that a named individual owns a specific number of shares in a company. It typically includes the company's seal, a certificate number, the share count, and signatures from corporate officers or a transfer agent. Historically, this piece of paper was the only proof of ownership that existed.

content.text: Why Almost Nobody Uses Them Anymore

content.html: Since the late 20th century, the stock market has shifted almost entirely to electronic book-entry ownership, where your brokerage account simply records that you own shares, with no paper involved. This system, run largely through the Depository Trust Company, is faster, cheaper, and eliminates the risk of losing or damaging a physical document that represents real money.

Today, when you buy a share of common stock or preferred stock through a brokerage, you almost never receive a paper certificate unless you specifically request one — and many companies have stopped issuing them at all.

content.text: Book-entry is the default now: If you bought stock through an online brokerage in the past twenty years, your shares almost certainly exist only as an electronic record — and that's entirely normal.
Do You Ever Actually Need One?

content.html: For nearly all practical purposes, no. Voting, receiving dividends, and selling shares all work fine through electronic registration. Some investors request physical certificates or Direct Registration System statements for sentimental reasons, as gifts, or because they simply prefer having proof outside the brokerage system, but it typically costs a fee and takes the shares out of easy, quick-trading form.

content.text: What to Do With an Old Certificate You Find

content.html: If you've inherited or discovered an old certificate, the first step is identifying whether the company still exists, was acquired, or changed its name — corporate actions like mergers and stock splits affect what the original shares are now worth. A stock transfer agent can research the certificate's status and help convert it back into modern electronic ownership if the underlying shares are still valid.

content.text: The Collectible Value of Old Certificates

content.html: Separate from any underlying share value, some old certificates have collectible worth on their own, particularly those with elaborate engraving, historical significance, or signatures from notable executives. A small community of collectors, known as scripophilists, buys and sells these documents purely for their design and history, sometimes paying far more than the shares themselves were ever worth as an investment.

Before assuming an old certificate is worthless simply because the company no longer trades under that name, it's worth checking both angles: whether the underlying shares survived a merger or reorganization, and whether the paper itself holds any collectible value independent of that.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• A stock certificate is a paper document proving you own a specific number of shares in a company.
  • Modern stock ownership is almost entirely electronic, tracked through book-entry systems rather than paper.
  • You can still request a physical certificate from some companies, usually for a fee.
  • Old certificates found among family papers may still represent real, tradeable value.
  • A transfer agent can research an old certificate's status and convert it to current electronic ownership.
  • Not having a paper certificate does not affect your legal ownership, voting rights, or dividend eligibility.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Are stock certificates still legally valid proof of ownership?

content.html: Yes, an authentic, unaltered certificate remains legal proof of ownership. But because most trading has moved to electronic systems, you'll typically need to work with a transfer agent to convert it into a tradeable book-entry position.

content.text: Can I still request a paper stock certificate today?

content.html: Some companies and transfer agents still offer this, often for a fee, but many companies have discontinued the practice entirely in favor of full electronic registration. Check with the specific company or your brokerage.

content.text: How do I find out if an old stock certificate is worth anything?

content.html: Contact the company's transfer agent, or a stock research service, with the certificate's details — company name, certificate number, and share count. They can trace whether the company still exists, merged, or was renamed, and what the shares are worth today.

content.text: Is it risky to hold a physical stock certificate instead of an electronic record?

content.html: It can be. A lost, stolen, or damaged certificate is harder and more expensive to replace than an electronic record, which is protected by your brokerage's systems and typically insured against certain losses.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Stock certificates aren't extinct, but they're no longer how ownership actually functions for the overwhelming majority of investors. If you own stock through a brokerage account today, your electronic record carries exactly the same legal weight as that old paper document once did — with far less risk of it getting lost in a drawer.

title: Circuit Breakers: How Exchanges Stop Market Crashes
excerpt: Circuit breakers are automatic rules that pause stock trading when prices fall too fast, giving markets a forced pause to prevent panic-driven spirals.

content.html: When markets plunge fast enough, exchanges don't just let the decline run — they stop it, on purpose, for a fixed number of minutes. That's what a stock market circuit breaker does: an automatic, rules-based pause triggered by steep, rapid price declines, designed to give traders a moment to absorb information rather than react purely on panic.

The system exists because of hard lessons learned from past crashes, and it now operates as a layered set of rules covering both the entire market and individual stocks, working alongside the exchange infrastructure described in how stock exchanges work.

content.text: Where the Rules Came From

content.html: Market-wide circuit breakers trace back to the crash of October 19, 1987, when the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell roughly 22% in a single day — the largest one-day percentage decline in its history. Regulators concluded afterward that a forced pause during extreme volatility could help prevent panic selling from spiraling further, and circuit breaker rules were introduced not long after and have been revised several times since.

content.text: The Three-Tier Market-Wide System

content.html: Today's market-wide circuit breakers are based on percentage declines in the S&P 500 index from the prior day's close, triggering different actions depending on severity.
Market-wide circuit breaker levels (S&P 500 decline from prior close)

rows: Trading halts for the remainder of the trading day

content.text: Timing matters: Level 1 and Level 2 halts don't trigger if the decline happens after 3:25pm Eastern — by that point in the session, the market is left to close on its own.
Single-Stock Circuit Breakers Work Differently

content.html: Beyond the market-wide system, individual stocks have their own "limit up-limit down" bands that pause trading in that specific stock if its price moves outside a defined percentage range within a short window. This targets stock-specific volatility — a bad earnings surprise or a trading error affecting one company — without needing to halt the entire market.

The allowable percentage band varies by how liquid and highly priced a stock is, with more actively traded, higher-priced stocks generally given tighter bands than smaller, thinly traded ones. If a stock's price threatens to move outside its band and stays there for a set number of seconds, trading in that single stock pauses briefly — typically around five minutes — even while the rest of the market keeps trading normally.

content.text: What Happens When Trading Resumes

content.html: After a halt, trading typically resumes through a special reopening auction, similar in spirit to the opening auction used at the start of a normal day, which aggregates pending orders to establish a new matched price rather than simply flipping trading back on all at once. This is meant to reduce the risk of a chaotic reopening after a volatile pause.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Circuit breakers automatically pause trading when the S&P 500 falls sharply within a single day.
  • The system traces back to the 1987 crash, when the Dow fell roughly 22% in one session.
  • There are three market-wide levels — 7%, 13%, and 20% declines — each triggering a different response.
  • A 20% decline halts trading for the rest of the day rather than a temporary pause.
  • Individual stocks also have their own limit up-limit down bands for stock-specific volatility.
  • Trading generally resumes through a reopening auction rather than an instant switch back on.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Have market-wide circuit breakers ever actually triggered?

content.html: Yes. They were triggered multiple times in March 2020 during the market volatility tied to the early COVID-19 pandemic, marking one of the few periods circuit breakers have activated since the modern rules were established.

content.text: Do circuit breakers apply to rising prices too?

content.html: Market-wide circuit breakers apply only to declines. However, single-stock limit up-limit down bands can pause a stock for moving too far in either direction, up or down, within a short window.

content.text: Can circuit breakers stop a stock from eventually falling further?

content.html: No — they only pause trading temporarily, giving the market a moment to absorb information. They don't prevent a decline from continuing once trading resumes if selling pressure persists.

content.text: Are circuit breaker rules the same on every exchange?

content.html: Market-wide circuit breakers apply across all U.S. exchanges simultaneously since they're tied to the S&P 500 index, so both the NYSE and Nasdaq halt together under the same triggers.

content.text: Do circuit breakers exist outside the United States?

content.html: Yes. Many major global exchanges use similar volatility-pause mechanisms, though the specific percentage thresholds, index references, and halt durations differ by country and regulator.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Circuit breakers are a deliberate design choice, not a bug in how markets work — a forced pause built directly into exchange rules so that extreme, fast-moving declines don't spiral purely on momentum and panic. They won't stop a genuine bear market from unfolding over weeks or months, but they've repeatedly given traders a brief, structured moment to reassess during the sharpest single-day drops.

faq.answer: Market-wide circuit breakers apply only to declines. However, single-stock limit up-limit down bands can pause a stock for moving too far in either direction, up or down, within a short window.

faq.question: Can circuit breakers stop a stock from eventually falling further?
faq.answer: No — they only pause trading temporarily, giving the market a moment to absorb information. They don't prevent a decline from continuing once trading resumes if selling pressure persists.

faq.question: Are circuit breaker rules the same on every exchange?
faq.answer: Market-wide circuit breakers apply across all U.S. exchanges simultaneously since they're tied to the S&P 500 index, so both the [NYSE](/financial-intelligence/nyse-explained) and [Nasdaq](/financial-intelligence/nasdaq-explained) halt together under the same triggers.

faq.question: Do circuit breakers exist outside the United States?
faq.answer: Yes. Many major global exchanges use similar volatility-pause mechanisms, though the specific percentage thresholds, index references, and halt durations differ by country and regulator.

title: Stock Market Trading Hours Explained
excerpt: U.S. stock exchanges run a regular session from 9:30am to 4pm Eastern, bookended by thinner, riskier pre-market and after-hours trading windows.

content.html: Ask when the stock market is open and most people know the rough answer: weekdays, during business hours. But stock market trading hours are more layered than that single window suggests, with distinct sessions that carry different rules, participants, and risks.
Knowing which session you're trading in matters because liquidity, the gap between bid and ask prices, and even how orders get matched can look meaningfully different outside the main session.

content.text: The Regular Session

content.html: Both the NYSE and Nasdaq run their regular trading session from 9:30am to 4:00pm Eastern Time, Monday through Friday, excluding designated market holidays. This is when trading volume and liquidity are at their highest, and it's when the opening and closing auctions discussed in NYSE explained occur.

content.text: Pre-Market and After-Hours Trading

content.html: Extended-hours trading lets investors place trades before the regular session opens (commonly from around 4:00am to 9:30am Eastern) and after it closes (commonly from 4:00pm to 8:00pm Eastern), though exact windows vary by broker. These sessions exist mainly so investors can react to news, like earnings releases, that companies often schedule before the open or after the close specifically to give the market time to digest them.

content.text: Extended hours carry real risk: Lower participation in pre-market and after-hours sessions means wider bid-ask spreads and thinner order books, so prices can swing more sharply on smaller trade volumes.
Why Liquidity Differs by Session

content.html: Far fewer market participants trade during extended hours compared to the regular session, which means the order book, covered in what is an order book, is typically thinner. That thinness is exactly why extended-hours price moves shouldn't always be read as a reliable preview of where a stock will open the next regular session — a large chunk of the market simply isn't participating yet.

content.text: Holidays and Early Closes

content.html: U.S. exchanges observe a set list of market holidays each year, such as New Year's Day, Independence Day, and Thanksgiving, when trading is fully closed, along with a handful of early-close days, like the day after Thanksgiving, when the regular session ends at 1:00pm Eastern instead of 4:00pm.

These schedules are published well in advance by the exchanges themselves, and brokers generally mirror them automatically, so an order placed on a holiday simply queues until the next open session rather than executing at some unexpected time.

content.text: Overnight Sessions and Global Markets

content.html: A newer development is limited overnight trading, offered by a handful of brokers and alternative trading venues that let investors place orders on U.S.-listed stocks well outside the traditional pre-market and after-hours windows. Volume in these sessions remains thin compared to the regular day, and prices set overnight can diverge noticeably from where a stock eventually opens once the full market is trading again.

It's also worth remembering that U.S. hours are just one piece of a global picture — European and Asian exchanges run on their own local schedules, and overlapping or non-overlapping hours between regions can influence how U.S. stocks with significant international revenue react to overnight news out of those markets.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• The regular U.S. stock market session runs 9:30am to 4:00pm Eastern Time, Monday through Friday.
  • Pre-market and after-hours sessions extend trading beyond the regular window but carry lower liquidity.
  • Wider bid-ask spreads and thinner order books make extended-hours price moves less reliable indicators.
  • Company earnings are often released before the open or after the close to give the market time to react.
  • U.S. exchanges observe fixed annual holidays plus occasional early-close days.
  • Regular-session trading offers the deepest liquidity and tightest spreads of any trading window.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Can I buy stocks 24 hours a day?

content.html: Not through standard U.S. exchange trading. Trading is limited to the regular session plus broker-supported pre-market and after-hours windows; some brokers now offer limited overnight sessions, but full 24-hour trading isn't standard across the market.

content.text: Is it riskier to trade in pre-market or after-hours sessions?

content.html: Generally yes. Lower participation means wider spreads, thinner order books, and prices that can move sharply on relatively small trade volumes, making execution less predictable than during the regular session.

content.text: What time zone are stock market hours based on?

content.html: U.S. exchange hours are set in Eastern Time, regardless of where an investor is physically located, so traders in other time zones need to convert accordingly.

content.text: Do all exchanges close on the same holidays?

content.html: U.S. exchanges like the NYSE and Nasdaq generally align their holiday and early-close schedules, though it's worth checking each exchange's published calendar since minor differences can occur in some years.

content.text: Why do some stocks move overnight even when U.S. markets are closed?

content.html: Overnight moves often reflect news from international markets, currency shifts, or futures trading that continues outside standard U.S. exchange hours, all of which can shape investor expectations before the next regular session even opens.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Trading hours aren't just a scheduling detail — they shape liquidity, spreads, and how reliably a price reflects broad market consensus. Sticking to the regular session generally means tighter spreads and deeper order books, while pre-market and after-hours trading offer flexibility at the cost of thinner, more volatile conditions.

title: Supply and Demand in the Stock Market
excerpt: Every stock price move ultimately traces back to supply and demand — how many shares are available to trade against how eager buyers and sellers are to trade them.

content.html: Economics 101 teaches supply and demand with lemonade stands, but the same logic runs the entire stock market, just with more moving parts. Supply and demand in the stock market determines whether a price rises or falls at any given instant, and understanding the specific factors that shift each side of that balance explains a lot of price behavior that otherwise looks random.

This sits one level below the mechanics covered in how and why stock prices change — supply and demand is the underlying economic force, while order matching is how that force actually gets translated into a traded price.

content.text: Supply: How Many Shares Exist and Are Available

content.html: A stock's supply starts with its total share count, set when the company goes public and adjusted afterward through actions like additional stock offerings, which increase supply, or share buybacks, which reduce it. Not every outstanding share is actively available to trade at any moment, though — insiders, large institutional holders, and index funds often hold shares for the long term, leaving a smaller "float" actually changing hands day to day.
A company that repurchases its own shares shrinks that available supply, which — all else equal — tends to support the price, since the same or greater demand is now chasing fewer available shares.

content.text: Demand: How Eager Buyers Are at Each Price

content.html: Demand reflects how many investors want to own a stock and how much they're willing to pay for it. That eagerness shifts with earnings results, growth prospects, interest rates, and plain sentiment — a strong product launch or a favorable analyst upgrade can pull in new buyers almost overnight, while a disappointing outlook can dry up demand just as fast.

content.text: Demand isn't just about buying interest: Rising demand only pushes the price up if it outpaces supply at the current price — a flood of buyers matched by an equal flood of sellers can leave the price essentially unchanged.
The Order Book Is Where Supply Meets Demand

content.html: In practice, supply and demand show up as a stack of pending buy and sell orders at different prices, tracked in what's called the order book — covered in detail in what is an order book. Every trade clears a layer of that stack, and the next best available price becomes the new frontier for buyers and sellers.

content.text: Why Supply Shocks Can Move Prices Fast

content.html: Sudden supply changes — a large institutional investor dumping shares, an unexpected secondary offering diluting existing shareholders, or a lockup period expiring after an IPO and releasing a wave of previously restricted shares — can move prices sharply even without any change in the underlying business, simply because the balance between available shares and existing demand has shifted abruptly.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Stock prices ultimately reflect the balance between available shares (supply) and buyer interest at each price (demand).
  • Share buybacks reduce supply and, all else equal, tend to support prices; new stock offerings increase supply and can pressure prices.
  • A stock's tradable float is often smaller than its total share count because many shares are held long-term.
  • Demand shifts with earnings, growth outlook, interest rates, and investor sentiment.
  • The order book is the real-time record of supply and demand meeting at specific price levels.
  • Sudden supply shocks, like lockup expirations or large block sales, can move prices sharply without any change to the business itself.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
Do share buybacks always increase the stock price?

content.html: Not automatically. Buybacks reduce the supply of tradable shares, which supports the price all else equal, but the overall price still depends on broader demand and market conditions at the time.

content.text: What is a stock's float?

content.html: Float refers to the shares of a company actually available for public trading, excluding shares held by insiders, founders, and other long-term holders who aren't actively buying or selling.

content.text: Why do stock prices drop after an IPO lockup expires?

content.html: Lockup periods restrict early investors and insiders from selling for a set time after an IPO. When that period ends, a sudden increase in available shares for sale can push supply up faster than demand, pressuring the price downward.

content.text: Is demand the same as trading volume?

content.html: No. Volume measures how many shares changed hands, not the direction of pressure. High volume can occur on both rising and falling days depending on whether buyers or sellers are more aggressive.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Supply and demand isn't an abstract textbook concept when it comes to stocks — it's the literal force that shows up in the order book every second the market is open. Watching for what changes each side of that balance, whether it's a buyback, a new offering, or a shift in investor sentiment, is often more useful than trying to predict price direction from headlines alone.

title: Support and Resistance Explained
excerpt: Support and resistance are price levels where a stock has repeatedly stalled or reversed — useful reference points, though far from guaranteed to hold.

content.html: Support and resistance describe price levels where a stock has repeatedly stopped falling or stopped rising in the past, and where traders expect — rightly or wrongly — that the same thing might happen again. Support sits below the current price and acts like a floor; resistance sits above it and acts like a ceiling. Neither is a hard rule of physics — they're really just zones where enough market participants have previously acted the same way that the pattern tends to draw attention.

content.text: Why These Levels Form at All

content.html: A support or resistance level typically forms because a meaningful number of traders bought or sold heavily at that price before. If a stock fell to $40 and bounced sharply, some investors who missed that entry will be waiting to buy again if it returns to $40, and some who bought exactly at $40 and are now underwater may sell to break even the next time the price gets back there. Both behaviors reinforce the level over time, at least until something changes the underlying story enough to overwhelm it.

content.text: How to Actually Spot a Level

content.html: The simplest method is visual: look for a price a stock has touched and reversed from at least twice, ideally with some time between touches. Round numbers — $50, $100, $200 — often act as psychological levels even without a specific chart history behind them, since order sizes and mental anchoring tend to cluster there. Previous highs and lows, especially ones that coincide with high trading volume, tend to carry more weight than levels touched only briefly.

content.text: Zones, not exact prices: Treat support and resistance as a range rather than a precise number — a level 'around $48 to $50' is usually more realistic than pretending the market respects $49.50 to the cent.
Role Reversal: When Support Becomes Resistance

content.html: One of the more consistently observed behaviors in this area is role reversal: once a support level breaks decisively, it often turns into resistance on the way back up, and the reverse happens when resistance breaks upward. The logic is similar to how the level formed in the first place — buyers who got trapped above a broken support level are often relieved just to sell around breakeven, which caps the bounce.

content.text: Where This Framework Breaks Down

content.html: Support and resistance levels fail constantly, and a 'false breakout' — where price briefly pierces a level and then reverses right back — is common enough that traders build entire strategies around waiting for confirmation rather than acting the instant a level breaks. Major news, earnings surprises, and broad market shifts can blow through a well-established level without hesitation, which is a useful reminder that these levels reflect past trader behavior, not any law about where a stock 'should' trade.

content.text: Using Support and Resistance With Other Tools

content.html: Levels become more useful when combined with other signals — a bounce off support that coincides with a bullish candlestick pattern or a rising trend line carries more weight than the level alone. This layered approach is standard practice across most of technical analysis, and it's covered in more general terms in our how to analyze a stock framework.

content.text: Key Takeaways

content.html:
• Support is a price floor where buying pressure has previously overwhelmed selling; resistance is the opposite ceiling.
  • Levels form because traders remember prior price action and tend to act similarly when price returns to it.
  • Round numbers and prior highs/lows with heavy volume tend to make more meaningful levels.
  • Broken support often becomes new resistance, and broken resistance often becomes new support — a pattern called role reversal.
  • False breakouts are common; many traders wait for confirmation before acting on a broken level.
  • Support and resistance work best combined with candlestick patterns, trend lines, and volume, not on their own.

content.text: Frequently Asked Questions
How exact should a support or resistance level be?

content.html: Treat it as a zone rather than an exact price. Markets rarely respect a level to the cent, so a range of a percent or two around the level is more realistic than pinpointing a single price.

content.text: What confirms a real breakout versus a false one?

content.html: A common approach is waiting for the price to close beyond the level, ideally on above-average volume, rather than reacting the instant it's touched intraday. Even then, false breakouts still happen and no confirmation method is foolproof.

content.text: Do support and resistance levels work on all timeframes?

content.html: The concept applies across timeframes, from minute charts to multi-year charts, but levels on longer timeframes are generally considered more significant since they reflect a broader consensus of trader behavior over time.

content.text: Why do stocks bounce off round numbers like $100?

content.html: Round numbers often act as psychological anchors — traders place orders around them, and options strike prices cluster there too, which can create real buying or selling pressure even without a specific chart history at that price.

content.text: Conclusion

content.html: Support and resistance give traders a simple visual framework for where a stock has previously found buyers or sellers, and role reversal — a broken level swapping function — is one of the more consistently observed patterns in this corner of technical analysis. None of it is guaranteed, though: false breakouts are routine, and any level can give way instantly to strong enough news. Use these levels as one input among several, not a standalone trading rule.
